utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31126 receives number P6707, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we're at break time and I expect to conclude my cross-examination shortly after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And, Mr. Stojanovic, we'd like to hear from the plans as far as the next witness is concerned. Not necessarily now. But, first of all, could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was not expecting that you had already communicated with Mr. Lukic, but I take it that you certainly will do so during the break. But you may have done it already. If there is anything to report, please let us know. Second, there was the other issue about you and Mr. Jeremy meeting during the break to find out whether I misstated that portion of the evidence where reference was made to crimes committed in relation to ethnicity of the victims. Anything to further report on that, either from you or from you, Mr. Jeremy?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, my understanding of the conversation is that the -- the translation of the relevant paragraphs is not disputed, and I also understand that it -- that we do not believe that you mischaracterised the paragraph in -- in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for having resolved that matter for me. Mr. Stojanovic, you agree with Mr. Jeremy?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is right, Your Honours. That is how matters stand. We just had a problem regarding the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm glad that that matter is resolved. We take a break and will resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While the witness will be brought in, any further reports from the Defence on the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours I would just like to inform you that during the break I contacted my colleague, Mr. Lukic. He is at the office right now and he is working with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I was asked to let you know and to ask for your understanding for the reasons why we were closer to the opinion that we had not -- we have not completed the proofing of the witness; namely, the witness testified in the Galic case, he does not speak English, and they are just going through the transcript of his testimony in the Galic case in order to complete the proofing. Last night when I was at the office together with my colleague, Mr. Lukic, and with the witness, we saw or I saw that there was a technical problem to open the map marked by the witness in the Galic case, which is a relevant piece of evidence because the data that he had when he was working at his duties in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps command, he marked the targets of the B and H army in Sarajevo itself. And so this morning they had to open it with the help of the technical service in order to go through that with the witness. Then once they searched the EDS, they did get a lot of documents which in the opinion of my colleague Mr. Lukic they need to go through in order to prepare the witness properly for his testimony because we believe that this is a very relevant witness. We did not have enough time last night or yesterday afternoon after court to complete this. This morning, they began again at 8.30 at the office, and as you could see I was in the courtroom by myself today with my colleague Mr. Saljic. So once again, we would kindly ask you to accept the reasons why we are not going to be able to bring the witness out today to begin his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber appreciates that you have explained the situation, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Jeremy, if you're ready, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dunjic, we -- we ended the last session discussing in some detail this incident between General Galic and yourself. Now, during his testimony in the Karadzic case, General Galic made a few comments about you, and I'd like to discuss those comments with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see on our screens 65 ter 31117. And this is the transcript of the testimony of Stanislav Galic in the Karadzic case. It's dated the 8th of May 2013. I would like to go to e-court page 14, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dunjic, as I mentioned, you were discussed by General Galic at various points during his testimony and -- actually, during his cross-examination, in particular, in the Karadzic case. Now, I'm going to read you an excerpt of that cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Before I read the excerpt, I can make a representation to the Court that while General Galic in the quote I'll read out to you refers --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: -- to you only as Dunjic, elsewhere in his testimony in the Karadzic case, he refers to you as "commander of the Igman Brigade, Dunjic," and that's at transcript page 37811, lines 6 to 7 in the Karadzic case. So I'll read the quotation and it's 22 lines of text, Mr. Dunjic, so please bear with me. "Q. Perhaps you could tell us whether Dunjic or Grkovic were removed" --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: "... for use of SRK artillery against Bosnian-held Sarajevo in a disproportionate fashion?" "A. The last assertion is correct about the two of them, and that's the words that I used, disproportionate use of firing assets, including artillery. I am an artilleryman. That's -- I meant artillery. And I said about Dunjic that he did lack discipline. And it's only normal when a war goes on. He was engaged. He had his own views as to how to deal with certain problems. I did not consider whether he was right or wrong in his theoretical considerations, but I had a lot of objections to the practical side of his use of assets. That's why I thought that he would -- should be removed and not to have to deal with the problem that existed in his area of responsibility, and also because he used artillery and firing assets in a disproportionate way. "When it comes to Grkovic, I don't know what Dunjic said here and I don't really care, to be honest. Let's be clear on that. I don't care what Dunjic said here. I know why a proposal was tabled for his removal. What he said is his problem. Everybody has the right to think for himself and to say whatever they want to say. That's the way he saw the problem, but I was the commander at the time. I had the right to make decision, and I proposed that he should be removed. I'm not hiding that. That is nothing new." Mr. Dunjic, do you have any comments on the fact that the reason why General Galic said that you were removed from your command was because you used artillery and firing assets in a disproportionate way?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: I am just now for the first time finding out that I used artillery disproportionately, and on the basis of documents you can see that while I was carrying out the duty as brigade commander I was never even once warned about unselective or disproportionate use of artillery. If Galic is an artilleryman, I'm a tank-man, and in the case of attack, the corps command was 100 kilometres away from my command. Lines were frequently cut. And in the event of an attack, I would use all available assets to destroy the enemy. That is correct. But I don't see what is disproportionate there. We were not playing chess. We were waging war. And Galic has the right to his opinion just as I have the right to mine. I didn't know that that was the reason. This is the first time that I'm hearing of it. I believe that the reason is actually the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: When you say "the incident," which incident -- can you be clear which incident you mean?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Of the 14th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: This was the incident in your apartment where you and General Galic had the altercation; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: At my forward command post in Hadzici. Yes, yes. Where we had the altercation, that's right, on the 14th of January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And do I understand your testimony correctly, which is that you were never -- General Galic never said to you that you were using artillery and firing assets in a disproportionate way; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Right. Not to me. Because he mentions me by name as the person who's using fire disproportionately.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So it's correct then that you dispute the truth about what General Galic is saying in his testimony in the Karadzic case; yes?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. First of all, I don't know what "disproportionate" means. I am a military man but I don't know what that means. I would like somebody to explain that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dunjic, it seems to be the case that regardless of how we define "disproportionate," it seems clear from General Galic's testimony that he had real concerns about the way that you were using artillery and firing assets. Did he ever bring those concerns to your attention?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Not to me personally, no. Some orders did arrive concerning all corps brigades and that was when there was a cease-fire that was agreed on not to use heavy weaponry. I do recall some orders about that. But nobody issued an order to me personally, neither orally or in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So from your answer, Mr. Dunjic, I interpret your answer as saying that when General Galic says that you were removed because you used artillery and firing assets in a disproportionate way, I understand your answer to be that, no, that is not in fact correct, that instead you were removed because of the event that happened on the 14th of January 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think, Mr. Jeremy, you are -- what the witness said is that he has no knowledge of any such reason for being removed and that he lives in the belief that the incident caused him to be removed and not anything else. That is. So what happened or not is not necessarily exactly the same of what the witness tells us of his awareness of the reasons for the removal. We should clearly distinguish the two. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dunjic, just to finally clarify my understanding: General Galic himself never personally drew to your attention concerns that he had regarding the use of artillery and firing assets regarding the way you were using them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jeremy. Mr. Stojanovic, have you any questions in re-examination for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have a few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dunjic, I'm asking you as a soldier: In the command and control system, who appoints and who relieves a commander of the brigade of duty?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the specific instance, you were replaced in late January 1993. Who specifically relieved you of duty?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: The corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you receive any written decision about this?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And who signed the decision on your dismissal from duty as commander of the Igman Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: I think it was either Marcetic or Galic. I don't recall the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether at any point General Mladic was directly informed about the incident of the 14th of January 1993?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at document 65 ter 31126 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is now P6707.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I didn't manage to write in the number. So please P6707.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document that you had the opportunity to see a while ago during the cross-examination. I'm just going to ask you to tell me whose document is this, judging by the heading?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: This is a document of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The document is signed by somebody who signed for the chief of the sector of the National Security Service, Predrag Ceranic?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that documents like this of the National Security Service were given to the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know if they were or were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And according to you, at any point in time because of events that occurred in Rajlovac and due to the arrest of two officers of the corps, were any disciplinary or criminal proceedings taken against you in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You answered a question of the Prosecutor by saying that although it was a long time ago, it was, in your opinion, a brilliant decision. Would you please tell us why you still think that is so after so many years?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: The positions of the Rajlovac Brigade were about to fall. The command in that brigade was completely in disarray. There was no commander of the brigade there. The chief of staff of the brigade was not there. They had abandoned their positions. Colonel Kosovac and Lieutenant-Colonel Maljkovic arrived in front of the corps command, or on behalf of the corps command, to deal with the situation. I came to Rajlovac, Colonel Kosovac was reporting to General Galic. He said, "General, sir, Dunjic arrived. The situation here has been resolved. Should Maljkovic and I now return to the corps?" The report of Colonel Kosovac to General Galic was false. The soldiers were abandoning their positions. They were throwing their weapons away. I made the decision on the spot to arrest those responsible for this situation, and the municipal leadership, following the logic that a soldier would say, "This man is arresting these guys. I wonder what will happen to us." I returned the units to their positions and saved the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And was this the period when a dominant feature, Zuc hill, was captured by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina during their assault?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was during that period. We're not just talking about Zuc but the line of separation. Let me explain to the Trial Chamber. The line of separation between the Rajlovac Brigade and the BiH Army forces was just 50 metres apart. With the fall of these dominant features, the whole municipality of Rajlovac would have fallen as well as the municipality of Vogosca. And the only road for thousands of civilians and members of six brigades -- actually, five brigades, not the Koseva Brigade, would be closed through Rajlovac, Vogosca, for Semizovac. All those units, together with the civilian populations, would have found themselves in an encirclement. These were positions where -- were such that if any brigade were to fall there would be a domino effect and all the other brigades would fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And let me finish by asking you whether you know that at that time people were arrested elsewhere including officers who were deemed to be responsible for everything what was happening to the positions of the Army Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: If you mean the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, yes. I knew that Colonel Josipovic in Vogosca arrested the command of the Vogosca Brigade due to their inability to organise combat. And the two of us did not do it in agreement. Both of us were taken by the military instinct to react immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up P1967. Page 6 in B/C/S and I believe it's the end of page 6 and the beginning of page 7 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dunjic, these are the minutes of the meeting which was held at the command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps which you attended, and Marko Lugonja has been recorded in this part addressing the gathering.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 6 in B/C/S and the following page in the English version of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The following page in B/C/S, page 6 and page 7 in English. Thank you. I believe that we have the correct pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you: Before I direct your attention to one part of this document, do you know -- did you know at the time about the Golf affair and the theft of cars from the TAS factory in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: I was aware of that, but let me explain that I became the brigade commander after the affair, when the whole thing was over. But I did know that there was a major theft in Vogosca, several thousand of cars had been stolen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to you, would that have been a major theft, a grand theft?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that before Marko Lugonja's introductory address? Did that theft precede that address?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that before you joined the unit and while you were there in Hadzici, Rajlovac, Vogosca, there were cases of illegal conduct, that the crime rate went up, that there was a lot of theft of property?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that that started happening before I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, who would have been in charge to prosecute such crimes that went on behind the brigades' lines?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: In my statement, I said that I filed dozens of criminal reports against my own soldiers for ammunition smuggling, for desertion, and other nonmilitary matters. Those criminal reports were sent to the judiciary bodies. The brigade commander is not in charge of actually processing such matters but only to file reports on learning that a crime had been committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at one paragraph together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In that paragraph you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, obviously you have not the corresponding pages on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that the B/C/S page is correct. As for the English version, we need to go back to the previous page and that would be the correct page in English. Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, this is not correct. This is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but I --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we moved twice. So if we -- well, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I think we go forward one more page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This I can't be the right page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. It -- we just had an English version where it was indicated the start of pages 6. Whenever it's on the screen, it disappears immediately. I don't know why. But let's try to get back. That's where in the English we see a 6 and that seems to correspond with ... Now, what part of page, and if I say "6," I mean 6 in the hard copy, would you like to draw our attention to, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In B/C/S we have the right page, paragraph starting with the wide phenomena of plunder and looting, and I believe it's on the following page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it's page 9 in e-court for the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Perhaps at the top of that page. Please, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that we are now on the right page, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dunjic, I would like to direct your attention to just one paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to thank Mr. Jeremy for his help.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Here, amongst others things, Mr. Lugonja says: "Extremely widespread theft, robbery, violence and other crimes. Everything is being stolen starting from cars, household appliances to clothing, et cetera. It is worth emphasising that many individuals feel that theft and robbery is their right and that it is the only way to be reimbursed for what they have lost or compensate for their participation in war." You participated in the events and you listened to this address. Did there come a time at any moment when this was happening only against non-Serbs or was this a widespread phenomenon involving everybody?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: It involves everybody, but I did not find myself in Mr. Lugonja's address. I didn't find parts of my unit in that address. And Mr. Galic also confirmed that in his report to the corps. He mentioned theft, robbery, and other things, whereas Mr. Galic in his report said that members behaved inappropriately, and he was referring to members of Brne's unit. If I do not say good morning to the Trial Chamber, I will not be behaving appropriately but this will not constitute a crime. So this wording "inappropriate behaviour" or "inappropriate conduct" may imply that he did not give the seat to an elderly woman a bus, but that doesn't imply crime, murders, killings, and any other forms of criminal behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you learn personally that in the area of responsibility of your brigade there were crimes which were committed by members of your unit against non-Serbian population?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: No. None of the units from my brigade. Including the members of the unit that is being referred to in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just try to. Mr. Stojanovic, did I understand you well that the extremely widespread theft, robbery, violence and other crimes, that you consider that to be crimes committed not specifically by the military but as a general feature of the time or did I misunderstand you? Was that the gist of your questions, that it was theft, robbery, everywhere, and not necessarily part of misbehaviour of the members of the Republika Srpska Army?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I read the document carefully while I was preparing to lead the witness, after having received it from the Prosecutor, I see that this refers to members of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps because this is how his address started, and that's why I asked Mr. Dunjic whether such occurrences were noticed in the area of responsibility of his unit behind his lines. And I meant not only soldiers but civilians as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just for me to properly understand, is it the position of the Defence that this document, and specifically this paragraph you took us to, also deals with crimes - that is, theft, robbery, violence, and other crimes - committed by others than the members of the SRK units? Is that your position or is it your position that this paragraph deals with criminal behaviour or at least misbehaviour of members of the SRK?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This refers to members of the SRK. The position of the Defence is that there were such occurrences among the civilian structure as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to explain something? This was the first such meeting from the moment combat activities started and it comprised all of the events that had taken place up to that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps for you, Mr. Dunjic, this part of this report, do you understand this to deal primarily, and I would even say exclusively, with misbehaviour of members of the SRK, or do you consider that this goes broader and also deals with crimes, et cetera, committed by others; civilians, nonmembers of the SRK?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I believe that this is the case. The others were prosecuted by the Ministry of the Interior or whatever was in charge. In any case, it wasn't the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But in this report --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But in this report, does that cover the -- well, let's say, the misbehaviour of members of the SRK or does, it in your view, go beyond that and does it cover crime in general, irrelevant whether it was committed by members of the SRK or any other person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this is a report from the field and involves other people who were not members of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps; i.e., civilians who were not engaged in any of the corps units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is just my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Almost every paragraph of -- almost every item in this paragraph specifically deals with military so therefore I'm a bit surprised by your explanation of this document, because every bullet point specifically refers to a military situation; ill-discipline for nonmilitary members. Discipline seems to be irrelevant. Nonrecognition of army hierarchy is not a matter which is primarily relevant for those who are not members of the armed forces. In third bullet point, they talk about units, which is also typically military language. And the fourth bullet point, where the theft, robbery, violence, and other crimes are mentioned. That's the only one -- well, it mentions that this is the -- that they consider it the only way to refund what they have lost or to compensate their participation in the war, which seems to be a rather military expression. The bullet point after that, whether they feel the Geneva and other conventions as obsolete and unnecessary is also usually what civilians would usually consider. The next bullet point deals with military police organs, which also is -- seems not to be very relevant for civilians. So in every bullet point, I find references to misbehaviour in a military situation. So therefore that surprises me that you say that this is a report which goes broader and also covers civilian abuse and civilian misbehaviour. If you have any comment on it, please give it. If not, then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I told you just a while ago that this was the first meeting of this kind which covered the period from the moment the conflict broke out in that territory to that meeting. It was not the military who stole cars from Vogosca and that's why I thought that this description refers to a wider range of people, not just members of the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In this paragraph, Vogosca is not even mentioned. Thank you. Any further questions, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dunjic, will you tell the Trial Chamber whether, when you discharged duties as the brigade commander, did you receive any instructions with regard to the treatment of humanitarian convoys on route to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. At another meeting, I received conclusions from a meeting, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber something about those conclusions?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Those conclusions were as follows: As far as I can remember, those convoys had to be led through. They had to be checked. And members of UNPROFOR were supposed to be treated correctly. In keeping with that order, I issued my own order and dispatched it to my subordinate units. I quoted the conclusions from that instruction that I received from my superior command; i.e., they were to treat UNPROFOR members fairly and correctly without any demonstration of hostility.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to call up 65 ter 14744. 14744.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you, Mr. Dunjic, to look at the document. It is dated 29 November 1992 in Blazuj. You can see that your name is printed and that the document was signed on your behalf by somebody whose signature is illegible.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: I can't read it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And it says here that you, as the brigade commander, order the implementation of conclusions and tasks reached at the meeting on the 17th November 1992 regarding the military situation and military behaviour. I am asking you whether you had in mind this document when you answered your previous question.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Further on, you say that the behaviour of members of your units - i.e., your subordinates - vis-à-vis UNPROFOR should be regulated according to the documents which is referred to herein. And you say under 4 that disciplinary measures should be taken including criminal responsibility for all mistreatment of UNPROFOR. And if they show ill-treatment towards our members of the military, that should be reported to our command. Did you have such situations?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And is this order of yours precisely the result of the conclusions of the advisory meeting?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I'm going to end with this question: At the advisory meeting, was anybody present from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska who would talk about it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: It was General Mladic and General Tolimir. They were there. General Mladic particularly drew attention, if I remember correctly, to this attitude or position towards members of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court according to your best recollection what exactly General Mladic said?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, the conclusions were precisely to behave professionally and in a fair way towards UNPROFOR members, not to permit the passage of weapons and ammunition in the area of responsibility of the units, but humanitarian aid, food and everything else had to be allowed to pass through without any problems regardless of whether it was in -- whether this was to Sarajevo. And as I mentioned, there was over 10.000 civilians who went through my area of responsibility from Sarajevo to Kiseljak. There were both citizens of Muslim and Croat ethnicity. So we did heed the orders of our general and we acted accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this document also. This is 65 ter document 14744.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 14744 receives number D607, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that would be everything that I had for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dunjic, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stojanovic, this document refers to a document dated the 17th of November, and this document also refers to a -- what seems to be the conclusions of a consultive meeting. Now, I think we have had a look at the minutes of a meeting which took place on the 15th of November. Is the 17th of November document, is that available to any party? Because it would create -- if it is about the same meeting, it would create a link between a meeting on the 15th, conclusions apparently put on paper on the 17th, and now the issuance of orders on the 29th but related to the conclusions reached or put on paper on the 17th of November. Is that document anywhere available?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will check that and I'll report back to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We are about to be at the conclusion of the testimony of this witness. Could an urgent search been done immediately? Or, Mr. Stojanovic, you've used this document. Perhaps you are aware of the document of the 17th of November. Meanwhile, while you're working on it I would have one question to the witness. Witness, what was the misbehaviour or the shortcomings in the attitude of -- towards UNPROFOR members? Could you tell us what had happened which triggered you to remind them that they should behave properly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At one time, we are talking about the Movtas Koras [phoen] facility that links Ilidza with Hadzici, at one of the check-points there, which was held by the public security service - I'm thinking about the Ministry of the Interior - two soldiers came from some special unit from Ilijas. They stopped the convoy. It was a mixed convoy -- actually, it was a French convoy that was entering Sarajevo. They were drunk, armed, and they verbally abused those who were in the convoy. Immediately upon finding out, I came to the location and with a special police unit, I -- maybe I made a mistake when I said they were from Vogosca. They were from Ilijas. So we took those two members of the army from that place and then immediately after that in light of the advisory meeting and the conclusions I drafted this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of what unit were these two members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were from the Ilijas Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the Savo Derikonja 1st Volunteer Detachment was a unit of what brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It belonged to the Igman Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because this order is directly addressed to this volunteer detachment, not to any unit of the Ilijas Brigade, so I have some difficulties in reconciling the reason why you said you issued this order, something that happened in the Ilijas Brigade, but you address a specific detachment - a volunteer detachment - in the Igman Brigade. Do you have any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do. Yes, I do. These orders, you can see in the right-hand corner it says: "To the command 1st volunteer detachment Savo Derikonja," that was the name of the unit. The order was sent to all of my units. I don't know why the other orders are not mentioned there, to the Rajlovac command, to the Rakovac Battalion command, to the command of the Blazuj Battalion, and the command of the Hadzici Battalion. So this order was not sent just to them but to all the units in my brigade in order to prevent what happened from happening again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if I look at the left bottom of this document, it is listed to whom this order was sent, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are these all the units in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the battalion command, 1 to 4, SSJB Ilidza, Hadzici, correct. Not to my brigade but they were at the check-points where the convoys passed, to the military police to my brigade, the Savo Derikonja Volunteer Detachment from my brigade, and the command of the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now the volunteer detachment is specifically mentioned. Did they have a special position within your brigade? Because they are not just subordinated to one of the battalion commands or any of the other units mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The brigade, by establishment, consists of battalions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he's saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat what you said. You started by saying that a brigade consists of battalions. Could you tell us what you then said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By establishment that was in force at the time, a brigade can also encompass detachments which are smaller than battalions but are of equal rank as the battalion. They are also subordinated to the brigade command and not to the command of a battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So this order to the -- this volunteer detachment has got nothing to do with what was discussed at the 15th of November and was not the subject of the 17th of November conclusions that were sent to you. Is that how I have to understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has any of the parties been able to identify and locate the 17th of November decision -- or conclusions, perhaps I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it appears that we are able to identify it. I do not see it currently uploaded in the e-court system. It does appear that we do have a translation for it, too, under ERN 05289502 to 059289505.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have a look at it? Is that a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, we can show the English translation on Sanction now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we could do so, please, if we could have a look at it, especially item 5. Yes. Could we go to the previous parts of it so that we have an opportunity to scan through it. First page, please. Could we further scroll down. It apparently is related to the 15th of November consultation meeting. Could we scroll further down, if my colleagues are -- could we scroll further down. Could we scroll further down. Could we scroll further down. Could we scroll further down. Could we scroll further down. Perhaps just a bit up at the beginning of paragraph 3. Could we scroll further down. Could we scroll further down. And the last page, please. And further down. This apparently is a document which is in between the meeting and preceding the further instructions given by this witness. We have seen this one document in which you complement the instruction given under number 5, that is to be kind to UNPROFOR. Did you give any further instructions on the basis of this document such as action to be taken against thefts or looting or criminal behavior? Did you issue any orders in that respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I issued the order in accordance with the conclusions of the advisory meeting regarding members of UNPROFOR. I did not issue orders regarding the looting, because it was not necessary. In the AOR of my brigade there were no such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if I understood you well, there were no such cases of unpleasant behaviour towards UNPROFOR within your brigade either, because you said it was triggered by something that happened in the Ilijas Brigade not the Igman Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You misunderstood me. This was committed by members of the Ilijas Brigade in the area of responsibility of my brigade. Two of them did it. They were at the Mostar crossroads, which is in the area of responsibility of my brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but they were not members of your brigade. I leave it to the parties whether they want to further deal with this document, yes or no. No further questions, Mr. Jeremy?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we tender that document that's now been uploaded, 65 ter 31172 -- oh, it will be. It will have that number. It's actually not in e-court yet. I think for the context of these discussions it makes sense to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection to the tendering of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no objection that it be tendered at presently for identification only until we receive the official translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could you already reserve a number for this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document that will be uploaded as 65 ter 31172 receives reserved number P6708, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And once it's uploaded, it will be marked for identification so that the Defence has a further opportunity to look at the original. No further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions. No further questions from the Bench, either. Mr. Dunjic, this concludes your testimony in this Court. I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague, it's a long way, and for having answered the many questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench and I wish you a safe return home again. You may --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank the Trial Chamber for having allowed me to testify on behalf of the Defence of the great Serbian hero --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- General Ratko Mladic. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No propaganda here. We have -- you are a witness. Mr. Mladic is in the courtroom and appears as an accused in this case. That is the situation at present. And your last expression of your feelings about the accused is part of the record of this trial and will be considered as every other word of your testimony by this Chamber. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to confirm that 65 ter 31172 is now in e-court, so I'd invite Mr. Stojanovic to check the translation and report back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: -- to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore it's marked for identification under number P6708.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We -- since there is no other witness at this moment, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least, Mr. Stojanovic, that's how we understood your explanation for the present situation, that the Defence is not in a position at this moment to call its next witness. For that reason, we'll adjourn for the day and we will resume on Monday the 1st of September 2014, 9.30 in the morning, hopefully in Courtroom I, but if not in a courtroom to be further announced. We stand adjourned.
